timeline.title: Baptised in Stratford
timeline.text: William was baptised on 26 April 1564. His exact birthday is not recorded; it is traditionally kept on 23 April. He was the third of eight children of John Shakespeare, a glover and alderman, and Mary Arden.

timeline.title: The grammar school
timeline.text: Most biographers think he went to the King's New School, Stratford's grammar school. No attendance records survive, so this is probable, not proven, and the years are not known.

timeline.title: Marriage to Anne Hathaway
timeline.text: A licence for William to marry Anne Hathaway was issued on 27 November 1582. He was 18 and she was 26.

timeline.title: A daughter, Susanna
timeline.text: Their first child, Susanna, was baptised on 26 May 1583.

timeline.title: Twins, Hamnet and Judith
timeline.text: Twins, a son Hamnet and a daughter Judith, were baptised on 2 February 1585.

timeline.title: The lost years
timeline.text: From 1585 to 1592 almost nothing is known about him, so scholars call these the "lost years". His name appears in a London law case in 1588 and 1589. Many stories about this time were told later and have no firm evidence.

timeline.title: "An upstart Crow"
timeline.text: The first surviving mention of his theatre work is an attack. In Groats-Worth of Wit (1592), the writer Robert Greene called him "an upstart Crow, beautified with our feathers", mocking an actor for daring to write plays. By then his early history plays were on stage.

timeline.title: Plague closes the theatres
timeline.text: Outbreaks of plague closed London's theatres for long periods in 1592 and 1593, cutting off the players' income.

timeline.title: Venus and Adonis
timeline.text: While the theatres were shut he wrote a long poem, Venus and Adonis, printed in 1593 by Richard Field, another man from Stratford. He dedicated it to the Earl of Southampton and called it "the first heir of my invention". It was reprinted fifteen times before 1640.

timeline.title: A sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men
timeline.text: From 1594 his plays were performed only by the Lord Chamberlain's Men, a company in which he was a sharer, or part-owner, as well as an actor and its main writer. They played at The Theatre in Shoreditch.

timeline.title: Romeo and Juliet and a Dream
timeline.text: Around 1595 he wrote Romeo and Juliet and A Midsummer Night's Dream. Exact dates for most of his plays are not known; scholars build them from printing records and clues in the texts.

timeline.title: Death of Hamnet
timeline.text: His only son, Hamnet, was buried on 11 August 1596, aged 11. The cause of death is unknown.

timeline.title: New Place
timeline.text: With his theatre earnings he bought New Place, the second-largest house in Stratford, for his family. He kept working in London and lodged there.

timeline.title: Taking The Theatre apart
timeline.text: In late December 1598, while the landlord was away, the carpenter Peter Street took apart the company's old playhouse, The Theatre, beam by beam. The timber was carried across the Thames to build a new one.

timeline.title: The Globe
timeline.text: The Globe opened in 1599 on the south bank of the Thames. It was owned by six sharers; Shakespeare held one eighth. He wrote Julius Caesar that same year.

timeline.title: Hamlet
timeline.text: Between about 1599 and 1601 he wrote As You Like It, Hamlet and Twelfth Night. A later tradition, not proven, says he himself played the ghost of Hamlet's father.

timeline.title: The King's Men
timeline.text: After Queen Elizabeth I died in 1603, the new king, James I, took the company under his own patronage, and it became the King's Men. Ben Jonson's records list Shakespeare acting in Jonson's play Sejanus that year.

timeline.title: Othello and Measure for Measure
timeline.text: By 1604 he rented rooms north of the river from Christopher Mountjoy, a French wigmaker. Around 1603 to 1604 he wrote Othello and Measure for Measure.

timeline.title: Plays at court
timeline.text: Between November 1604 and October 1605 the King's Men performed seven of his plays at court. In 1605 he also invested in a share of Stratford's parish tithes.

timeline.title: The great tragedies
timeline.text: Around 1605 and 1606 he wrote King Lear, Macbeth and Antony and Cleopatra. For Antony and Cleopatra he worked closely from Thomas North's 1579 English translation of Plutarch.

timeline.title: An indoor theatre
timeline.text: In 1608 the King's Men took over the Blackfriars, an indoor theatre, as a second home beside the open-air Globe.

timeline.title: The Sonnets in print
timeline.text: Thomas Thorpe published 154 sonnets under Shakespeare's name in 1609. They were written over many years, and nobody knows if Shakespeare agreed to the printing.

timeline.title: The Tempest
timeline.text: Around 1610 to 1611 he wrote The Tempest, one of his late plays often called romances.

timeline.title: The Globe burns
timeline.text: During a performance of Henry VIII, a play he probably wrote with John Fletcher, a stage cannon set the thatched roof on fire. The Globe burned down, but no one was seriously hurt. It was rebuilt in 1614 with a tiled roof.

timeline.title: Home to Stratford
timeline.text: Around 1613 he seems to have retired to Stratford, though in March 1613 he also bought a gatehouse in London's Blackfriars. His last plays were probably written with John Fletcher.

timeline.title: His will
timeline.text: He signed his will on 25 March 1616. He left his wife his "second best bed", a line scholars still argue about.

timeline.title: Death in Stratford
timeline.text: Shakespeare died on 23 April 1616, aged 52, and was buried in Holy Trinity Church two days later. His gravestone warns: "cursed be he that moves my bones". A monument showing him writing was put up in the church before 1623.

timeline.title: The First Folio
timeline.text: His fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell collected 36 of his plays in one book, the First Folio. Eighteen of them were not known to have been printed before. About 235 copies survive.

timeline.title: A fringe question
timeline.text: From the mid-1800s some people claimed that someone else wrote his works. Nearly all scholars treat this as a fringe theory; the records of his life and career point to Shakespeare of Stratford.

timeline.title: The Globe returns
timeline.text: A reconstruction, Shakespeare's Globe, opened in 1997 about 230 metres from the original site. His plays are still performed there and around the world.

works.title: Henry VI and Richard III
works.text: His early history plays about the Wars of the Roses, written around 1591 to 1593.

works.title: Venus and Adonis
works.text: A long narrative poem written while plague closed the theatres, and a bestseller of its time.

works.title: Romeo and Juliet
works.text: A tragedy of two young lovers from feuding families in Verona.

works.title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
works.text: A comedy of lovers, fairies and a group of working men putting on a play.

works.title: Henry IV, Part 1
works.text: A history play about a young prince and his friend Falstaff, written around 1596 to 1597.

works.title: The Globe Theatre
works.text: The open-air playhouse his company built in 1599, with Shakespeare as one of six owners.

works.title: Julius Caesar
works.text: A Roman tragedy about power, loyalty and persuasion, written for the new Globe.

works.title: As You Like It
works.text: A comedy set in the Forest of Arden, written around 1599 to 1600.

works.title: Hamlet
works.text: A tragedy about a prince who must decide whether to avenge his father, written around 1599 to 1601.

works.title: Twelfth Night
works.text: A comedy of shipwrecked twins and mistaken identity.

works.title: Othello
works.text: A tragedy of jealousy and trust, written around 1603 to 1604.

works.title: King Lear
works.text: A tragedy about an old king who divides his kingdom among his daughters, written around 1605 to 1606.

works.title: Macbeth
works.text: A short, fast tragedy about ambition and guilt in Scotland.

works.title: Antony and Cleopatra
works.text: A Roman tragedy built closely on North's translation of Plutarch.

works.title: The Sonnets
works.text: 154 fourteen-line poems on love, time and art, printed by Thomas Thorpe.

works.title: The Tempest
works.text: A late romance about a magician on an island who chooses forgiveness, written around 1610 to 1611.

works.title: Henry VIII and The Two Noble Kinsmen
works.text: Late plays he probably wrote together with John Fletcher.

works.title: The First Folio
works.text: The collected edition of 36 plays, put together by his fellow actors after his death.
